messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 67-year-old widowed military medic, has been struggling with significant symptoms following a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The event occurred while he was driving home one evening; another driver swerved into his lane under the influence of alcohol, causing a catastrophic crash that left John badly injured. Since then, simple things like the smell of alcohol or burnt rubber have become potent triggers for John. He often finds himself jolted out of his routine by these olfactory cues, which immediately activate intense physical reactions and make him feel incredibly vulnerable. When he encounters the scent of burning, it's as if the accident is replaying in his mind, and he feels jumpy and easily startled. John’s memories of the event are disjointed and fragmented. He struggles to articulate what happened coherently; when he tries to explain it, he often loses the thread of his narrative. The memory itself can feel like it belongs to someone else, further complicating his ability to process the trauma. When these intrusive recollections surface, they’re accompanied by auditory hallucinations—sounds from the crash replaying in his head. John’s self-blame has been relentless since the accident. He believes that if he had acted differently or more cautiously, he could have prevented the collision. This self-doubt and belief in his own weakness have led him to adopt various maladaptive strategies as a way of coping. He constantly monitors his thoughts for signs of going crazy and tries to suppress any recollections of the trauma. These behaviors only intensify his sense of vulnerability and trigger more physical reactivity. The fear that he is weak and unable to handle such situations has made John avoid driving altogether, which has had significant consequences on both his personal life and professional work as a medic. He finds himself struggling to respond effectively in emergency scenarios because the mere thought of being behind the wheel or even being a passenger can set off a cascade of negative emotions. His maladaptive strategies have also exacerbated his memory issues. The more he tries to push thoughts away, the more intrusive they become, leading him into a cycle where each trigger sets off a series of reactions that reinforce his negative appraisals and further diminishes his confidence in handling stressful situations. The constant monitoring and suppression have taken a toll on John's mental health, and it has affected his relationships with friends and family. His son had to take over as the primary caregiver for his late wife’s memory box, which is filled with photographs and mementos from their marriage—a task that used to bring him comfort but now only serves as another reminder of the accident. What finally brought John to seek help was a recent episode where he experienced a severe panic attack at work after hearing sirens. He realized then that his maladaptive strategies were no longer sustainable and feared they would lead to more severe consequences, including a complete breakdown in his ability to function professionally and personally. John is most afraid of becoming completely incapacitated by his symptoms and unable to care for himself or support those he loves. He hopes that with therapy, he can regain control over his life and feel less vulnerable, so he can once again be the person who provides comfort and security rather than feeling like a burden to others.
